title: Improved State Mixing in Higher-order and Block Diagonal Linear Recurrent Networks
claim: Structured state mixing yields higher accuracy at lower compute than diagonal and dense recurrent baselines, with an optimal mixing size.
layout: 4 panels: small schematics left, large scatter center, two line plots right
description: A composite figure with four panels. Panel A, at top left, is a small sketch of two crossing curved arrows labeled efficiency and expressivity over a block size axis, with three small grids of increasing colored density beneath it. Panel B shows block-diagonal gate matrices for H-LRU and BD-LRU. Black cells are identity gates, white cells are zero gates, and colored cells are selective gates, with orange outlines and a narrow column for the input gates. Panel C is the large center scatter plot titled Performance of leading models. FLOPs per recurrent step on a log x-axis are plotted against mean accuracy on the y-axis. Colored dots mark the models, and arrows labeled ours point to BD-LRU at the top left, H-LRU and diagonal LRU. A legend lists the models. Panel D, at right, has two dashed line plots of accuracy against window size and block size, each peaking at a moderate size. The eye goes first to the green BD-LRU dot at the top of panel C.
caption: Structure and performance of the proposed H-LRU and BD-LRU architectures. A. A schematic illustration of the theoretically predicted trade-off between expressivity and efficiency of block-diagonal linear recurrent networks. B. Schematic illustration of the gating mechanisms in block-diagonal form, showing both the state gates that constitute the state-transition matrix and the input gates that act on external inputs. The structure of the gates’ selectivity is color-coded: white squares indicate fixed zero gates, black squares indicate fixed identity gates, other colors indicate active selective gates; similar color palettes indicate row-wise normalization. C. Summary of the performance of the proposed and the baseline models. The x-axis indicates the number of FLOPs per recurrent step. The y-axis denotes the mean test accuracy over all considered synthetic tasks (compression, selective copying, in-context recall, permutation) of the overall best-performing model configuration (hidden size up to 6k). Optimal hidden sizes vary between models, see also Fig. 12. Note that H-LRU and BD-LRU can achieve better or matching performance than both linear and nonlinear baselines while requiring fewer FLOPs per recurrent step. Diagonal LRU reports the best results across both H-LRU m1 and BD-LRU m1, which are identical for m = 1. D. Best performance for different window sizes m (H-LRU) and block sizes m (BD-LRU).
abstract: Linear recurrent networks (LRNNs) and linear state space models (SSMs) promise computational and memory efficiency on sequence modeling tasks, yet their diagonal state transitions limit expressivity. Dense and/or nonlinear architectures (e.g., LSTMs) on the other hand are provably more expressive, but computationally costly. Here, we explore how expressivity in LRNNs can be increased via richer state mixing across time and channels while maintaining competitive efficiency. Specifically, we introduce two structured LRNN architectures: (i) Higher-order Linear Recurrent Units (H-LRU), which generalize recurrences to arbitrary order, mixing multiple past states, and (ii) Block-Diagonal LRUs (BD-LRU), which enable dense intra-block channel mixing. To ensure stable training, we introduce a selective gate normalization scheme that allows for scalable window and block sizes. To maintain efficiency, we implement block-diagonal parallel scans in PyTorch and Triton that keep the throughput competitive with diagonal LRNNs for moderate orders (H-LRU) and block sizes (BD-LRU). Consistent with prior theoretical studies on the limitations of diagonal models, we empirically demonstrate that our architectures benefit from the increased expressivity of structured state mixing, on synthetic sequence modeling and on language modeling tasks that require tracking structure. Our results show that the structure of state mixing is a critical driver of performance in LRNNs, offering a practical pathway to closing the efficiency-expressivity gap in linear sequence models.
